criteria.evidence: native/browser/manifest.toml pins the Windows target, CEF/Chromium/cef-rs versions, archive hashes, ABI, protocol and notices.
The signed runtime and same-version development archive were verified on Windows 11 build 26200.0; the manifest declares the Windows 10 1809 floor and bootstrap, sandbox and control-only contracts.
scripts/fetch-browser.py returned VERIFIED for the pinned signed archive and the fetch security suite passed 12/12.
The common browser contract commit and protocol version are recorded in the target manifest.
Fetch negative-path tests cover absent, mismatched, unsafe and incompatible artifacts while preserving an existing verified runtime.
The Windows client exports RunWinMain, receives sandbox_info, keeps sandboxing enabled and does not use browser_subprocess_path.
Bootstrap/client roles, PE checks, export checks and unknown-DLL refusal are wired in the Windows readiness contract.
The pinned client was built with the same-version CEF development archive, staged with the signed runtime, locally signed for qualification, and executed through the real bootstrap handshake.
CEF remains absent from terminal startup and is loaded only through Browser activation and the Windows supervisor.
Missing runtime, incompatible ABI, invalid PE and missing export paths fail closed as Browser unavailable.
Named-pipe ACLs are owner-scoped and descendant ownership uses a KILL_ON_JOB_CLOSE Job Object without inherited control handles or process-name kills.
Windows profile tests passed 6/6; production profile creation applies protected SYSTEM, administrators and owner ACLs, and the native receipt reports exactly those entries.
Root locking, ownership, routing, handshake, closure and refused readiness paths are wired and the Windows supervisor contract tests passed 4/4; the native control round trip completed successfully.
Process handles and the owned Job Object control the lifetime; shutdown is bounded and does not elevate privileges or kill by process name.
Readiness, parent-loss and supervisor failures route to Browser errors while preserving terminal startup and existing profile state.
The platform registry selects the Windows adapters while reusing the shared Browser controller, dock, owners, profiles, descriptors and lifecycle.
The deterministic shared controller path is wired to the Windows ProfileHost and native v3 create/close protocol; no Windows-specific dock rewrite exists.
The target remains development-only and control-only; invalid or absent runtime data leaves public activation unavailable.
The Windows adapters consume the recorded common contract and protocol rather than duplicating the Linux dock implementation.
